title: Can Claude turn my notes into a full TRANSCRIPT of the meeting?
text: Someone assumes board minutes means a full transcript of everything that was said. Wrong word. Minutes are the record of what was decided, not what was said. Lay them, take them through it. It's tempting to think a fuller draft is a

title: A private doubt, permanently recorded
text: Better draft, every comment, every aside captured. But say the notes include a director's offhand doubt about a deal, later dropped without a vote. Minutes that recorded it would preserve a private hesitation as a permanent record attached to a decision that was never actually made. Real board minutes leave it out on purpose. They record decisions and actions, not discussion. A minutes

title: Three parts — the anchor
text: Handoff that actually works is three parts. Raw notes in, a draft limited to decisions, motions, and actions out, and a required approval step before any of it counts as official. title: Draft, then approved
text: Back to the board at the next meeting, gets checked line by line against what was actually decided, and only once the board votes to approve it does it become the official minutes. But a draft nobody marked up isn't automatically approved. Silence isn't a vote. The board still has to say yes. And a draft that gets heavily corrected at approval isn't a failure either.
